11. Question

Which two statements are true about the SET VERIFY ON command? (Choose two.)

  • 1.
  • 2.
  • 3.
  • 4.
  • 5.
Correct

Correct

Option A. It can be used in SQL Developer and SQLPlus*

  • Correct because SET VERIFY ON is supported in both SQLPlus* and SQL Developer.
  • It controls whether substitution variables are displayed after replacement, helping users verify the values being used in queries.

Option B. It displays values for variables created by the DEFINE command

  • Correct because SET VERIFY ON shows the old and new values of substitution variables (created with DEFINE or referenced with &).
  • This helps confirm that variable substitution is happening as expected.

Incorrect

Option C. It displays values for variables prefixed with &&

  • Incorrect because && variables are substitution variables that persist for the session, but SET VERIFY ON does not specifically target them.
  • It applies to all substitution variables, not just &&.

Option D. It displays values for variables used only in the WHERE clause of a query

  • Incorrect because SET VERIFY ON applies to substitution variables anywhere in the SQL statement, not limited to the WHERE clause.

  • Incorrect because SQL Developer also supports SET VERIFY ON.
  • Limiting it to SQL*Plus is inaccurate.

questions.preview: Which three statements are true regarding indexes? (Choose three.)
questions.question_html:
Question 12 of 60
12. Question

Which three statements are true regarding indexes? (Choose three.)

  • 1.
  • 2.
  • 3.
  • 4.
  • 5.
  • 6.
Correct

Correct

Option A. An update to a table can result in no updates to any of the table’s indexes

  • Correct because if the update does not affect any indexed columns, then no index entries need to be updated.
  • Example: Updating a non‑indexed column leaves all indexes unchanged.

Option B. A SELECT statement can access one or more indices without accessing any tables

  • Correct because Oracle can satisfy queries entirely from an index if the index contains all the required columns (known as a covering index).
  • This reduces table access and improves performance.

Option F. A table belonging to one user can have an index that belongs to a different user

  • Correct because indexes can be created in a different schema than the table, provided the user has the necessary privileges.
  • This allows separation of ownership between tables and indexes.

Incorrect

Option C. An update to a table can result in updates to any or all of the table’s indexes

  • Incorrect because only indexes on the columns being updated are affected.
  • Not all indexes are updated automatically; only those tied to modified columns.

Option D. A UNIQUE index can be altered to be non‑unique

  • Incorrect because uniqueness is a fundamental property of the index.
  • You cannot alter a UNIQUE index to make it non‑unique; you must drop and recreate it.

Option E. When a table is dropped and is moved to the RECYCLE BIN, all indexes built on that table are permanently dropped

  • Incorrect because when a table is dropped into the Recycle Bin, its dependent objects (including indexes) are also moved to the Recycle Bin, not permanently dropped.
  • They can be restored with the FLASHBACK TABLE command.

Correct

Option D. Rows moved starting from the beginning of the segment

Correct

  • Correct because DBTIMEZONE shows the database’s time zone setting, which can be expressed as an offset from UTC (e.g., +05:30).

  • Correct because values are normalized to the database time zone when stored, but displayed in the session’s local time zone. This ensures consistency across sessions.

Question 16 of 60
16. Question

Which three statements are true about undo segments and the use of undo by transactions in an Oracle database instance? (Choose three.)

  • 1.
  • 2.
  • 3.
  • 4.
  • 5.
  • 6.
Correct

Here are the three true statements:

  1. An undo segment may be used by multiple transactions simultaneously.

    • Multiple transactions can utilize the same undo segment concurrently. The database manages the allocation and deallocation of undo space efficiently to accommodate multiple active transactions.

  2. Undo segments can extend when a transaction fills the last extent of the undo segment.

    • If a transaction requires more undo space than is currently allocated to an undo segment, the segment can automatically extend by adding more extents. This ensures that sufficient undo space is available for the transaction to complete.

  3. Undo segments can wrap around to the first extent when a transaction fills the last extend of the undo segment.

    • When a transaction fills the last extent of an undo segment, the database can reuse the space in the first extent, effectively allowing the undo segment to “wrap around.” This is a common technique for managing undo space efficiently, especially in high-transaction environments.

Correct

Option B.

  • Correct because of operator precedence in SQL.
  • AND has higher precedence than OR.
  • So the condition is interpreted as:

    (borrowed_date = SYSDATE AND transaction_type = 'RM') 
OR member_id IN ('A101', 'A102');
  • This matches the logical grouping in Option D.

Option D.

  • Correct because it explicitly groups the condition:
    sql
    (borrowed_date = SYSDATE AND transaction_type = 'RM') 
OR member_id IN ('A101', 'VA102');

Question 18 of 60
18. Question

You execute this command: During the export operation, you detach from the job by using CTRL+C and then execute this command:

sql
Export> STOP_JOB=immediate -
Are you sure you wish to stop the job ([yes]/no): yes

Which two statements are true about the job? (Choose two.)

  • 1.
  • 2.
  • 3.
  • 4.
  • 5.
Correct

Correct

Option A. It is paused and can be resumed

  • Correct because STOP_JOB=immediate halts the Data Pump job immediately, but does not terminate it.
  • The job is placed in a stopped state, allowing you to later resume it using START_JOB.
  • This ensures that the export can continue from where it left off.

Option D. You can reattach to it and monitor it

  • Correct because Data Pump jobs are server-side jobs.
  • Even after detaching with CTRL+C and stopping the job, you can reattach to it using the ATTACH command.
  • This allows monitoring or resuming the job after it has been paused.

Incorrect

Option B. It continues to run in the background

  • Incorrect because the STOP_JOB=immediate command explicitly stops the job.
  • It does not continue running in the background.

Option C. It terminates

  • Incorrect because termination would mean the job is destroyed and cannot be resumed.
  • Here, the job is only paused, not terminated.

Option E. You can no longer monitor it

  • Incorrect because you can still reattach and monitor the job.
  • Data Pump jobs remain accessible until explicitly terminated.

Correct

    • transaction_date AS DATE is valid since DATE is treated as an alias when quoted.
    • Arithmetic expression amount + 100 "DUES" is valid with aliasing.
  • This query executes successfully.

Option E.

  • Correct because:
    • Aliases can be defined without AS (e.g., customer_id CUSTID).
    • transaction_date TRANS_DATE is valid shorthand aliasing.
    • amount + 100 DUES is also valid aliasing.
  • This query executes successfully.

Incorrect

Option B.

  • This causes a syntax error.

Option D.

  • Incorrect because single quotes ('CUSTOMER-ID') are not valid for column aliasing in Oracle SQL.
  • Single quotes denote string literals, not identifiers.

Which two statements are true regarding indexes? (Choose three.)

  • 1.

Correct

Option B. An update to a table can result in no updates to any of the table’s indexes

  • Correct because if the update does not affect indexed columns, then no index entries need to be modified.
  • Example: Updating a non‑indexed column leaves all indexes untouched.

Option D. A table belonging to one user cannot have an index that belongs to a different user

  • Correct because indexes are schema objects owned by the same user who owns the table.
  • Oracle does not allow cross‑ownership of indexes.

  • Correct because if the update modifies indexed columns, then the corresponding indexes must be updated.

  • You must drop and recreate the index as unique.

  • Incorrect because when a table is dropped and moved to the recycle bin, its dependent indexes are also dropped and can appear in the recycle bin.

22. Question

Which two statements are true about the BIG_TBS tablespace? (Choose two.)

  • Option A. It must be bigger than the largest SMALLFILE tablespace
  • Option B. It will always have a 32K blocksize
  • Option C. It will be a dictionary-managed tablespace by default
  • Option D. AUTOEXTEND is possible for the datafile

  • 1.

Correct

Correct

  • Option A. It must be bigger than the largest SMALLFILE tablespace → Correct because a BIGFILE tablespace is designed to support extremely large storage sizes compared to SMALLFILE tablespaces. By definition, BIGFILE tablespaces can contain a single datafile that is much larger than any SMALLFILE tablespace.
  • Option D. AUTOEXTEND is possible for the datafile → Correct because BIGFILE tablespaces support AUTOEXTEND functionality. This allows the single large datafile to grow automatically as needed, provided sufficient storage is available in the filesystem.

Incorrect

questions.preview: Which statements are true about service names used to connect to an Oracle Datab
questions.question_html:
Question 1 of 20
1. Question

Which statements are true about service names used to connect to an Oracle Database instance? (Choose three)

  • 1.
  • 2.
  • 3.
  • 4.
  • 5.
  • 6.
Correct

Correct:

B. Database instances can register a service name with multiple listeners on the same host.

This statement is correct. If you have multiple listeners configured on the same host, an Oracle database instance can register its services with all of them. This provides redundancy and load balancing capabilities among listeners on that particular host. This is configured by having the LOCAL_LISTENER and/or REMOTE_LISTENER parameters point to multiple listener endpoints.

D. Database instances can register a service name with multiple listeners on different hosts.

This statement is correct. Through the use of the REMOTE_LISTENER initialization parameter, a database instance can register its services with listeners residing on different hosts. This is fundamental for Real Application Clusters (RAC) environments and for achieving high availability and load balancing across nodes.

F. Service names can be statically defined for a listener.

This statement is correct. While dynamic registration (using PMON and LOCAL_LISTENER/REMOTE_LISTENER parameters) is the preferred and default method for active services, service names can also be statically defined in the listener.ora file. This is often necessary for:

Databases that are not automatically registering (e.g., older versions, or specific configurations).
When a database instance is not running and you want the listener to still report its existence (though it won‘t be connectable).
For specific administrative connections where dynamic registration might not yet be complete.
Incorrect:

A. A service name can be specified only in connect descriptors in a TNSNAMES.ORA file.

This statement is incorrect. While tnsnames.ora is a common method, service names can also be resolved through other naming methods, such as:

Easy Connect Naming: hostname:port/service_name (no tnsnames.ora needed).
Directory Naming: Using an LDAP directory server (like Oracle Internet Directory or Microsoft Active Directory).
External Naming: Using NIS or other third-party naming services.
E. A service name can be specified only in one connect descriptor in a TNSNAMES.ORA file.

This statement is incorrect. A single service name can appear in multiple connect descriptors within the same tnsnames.ora file. This is typically done to configure client-side load balancing or failover. For example, a single SALES service name could have multiple addresses listed, allowing the client to try connecting to different listeners for the SALES service.

When a database instance is not running and you want the listener to still report its existence (though it won‘t be connectable).
For specific administrative connections where dynamic registration might not yet be complete.
Incorrect:

A. A service name can be specified only in connect descriptors in a TNSNAMES.ORA file.

This statement is incorrect. While tnsnames.ora is a common method, service names can also be resolved through other naming methods, such as:

Easy Connect Naming: hostname:port/service_name (no tnsnames.ora needed).
Directory Naming: Using an LDAP directory server (like Oracle Internet Directory or Microsoft Active Directory).
External Naming: Using NIS or other third-party naming services.
E. A service name can be specified only in one connect descriptor in a TNSNAMES.ORA file.

This statement is incorrect. A single service name can appear in multiple connect descriptors within the same tnsnames.ora file. This is typically done to configure client-side load balancing or failover. For example, a single SALES service name could have multiple addresses listed, allowing the client to try connecting to different listeners for the SALES service.

questions.preview: Which statements are true about UNDO and REDO? (Choose two)
questions.question_html:
Question 4 of 20
4. Question

Which statements are true about UNDO and REDO? (Choose two)

  • 1.
  • 2.
  • 3.
  • 4.
  • 5.
Correct

Correct

Option B. REDO and UNDO are both written by the Log Writer process (LGWR).

  • The Log Writer (LGWR) process is responsible for writing redo entries to the redo log files.
  • UNDO information is also recorded in redo logs to ensure recovery consistency.
  • This ensures that both committed and uncommitted transactions can be recovered properly.

Option D. UNDO is used when a ROLLBACK statement is issued.

  • UNDO records store the before‑image of data changes.
  • When a ROLLBACK is executed, Oracle uses UNDO to restore the data to its previous state.
  • This is a fundamental purpose of UNDO in transaction management.

Incorrect

Option A. UNDO is used when a COMMIT statement is issued.

  • At COMMIT, UNDO is not used; instead, REDO ensures durability of changes.
  • UNDO is only relevant for rolling back or providing read consistency, not for commit operations.

Option C. UNDO is generated by the creation of REDO when tables are modified.

  • UNDO and REDO are separate concepts.
  • UNDO stores before‑images for rollback, while REDO stores after‑images for recovery.
  • One is not generated by the other.

Option E. REDO is generated by the creation of UNDO when tables are modified.

  • Again, this is incorrect.
  • REDO is generated for changes made to data blocks, not because UNDO is created.
  • Both are generated independently to serve different recovery purposes.

questions.preview: Which statements are true about constraints and indexes? (Choose three)
questions.question_html:
Question 5 of 20
5. Question

Which statements are true about constraints and indexes? (Choose three)

  • 1.
  • 2.
  • 3.
  • 4.
  • 5.
  • 6.
Correct

Correct:

D. A foreign key value in a child table column must match a key value in its parent table‘s primary or unique key column.

This statement is correct. This is the fundamental definition of a foreign key constraint. It enforces referential integrity, ensuring that a value in the foreign key column(s) of the child table either matches an existing value in the primary or unique key column(s) of the parent table, or is NULL (unless the foreign key column is also defined as NOT NULL).

E. Unique constraints permit NULLs in the constrained column.

This statement is correct. A unique constraint ensures that all values in the constrained column (or set of columns) are unique. However, unlike a primary key constraint, a unique constraint does allow NULL values. If NULL values are permitted, multiple rows can have NULL in the unique column, as NULL is considered “unknown“ and not equal to any other value, including another NULL.

F. Primary Key constraints can be added to an already indexed column if the existing index is unique.

This statement is correct. When you create a PRIMARY KEY constraint on a column (or set of columns), Oracle automatically creates a UNIQUE INDEX on those columns if one doesn‘t already exist. If a unique index already exists on the column(s) that you are designating as the primary key, Oracle can simply use that existing unique index to enforce the primary key constraint, rather than creating a new one.

Incorrect:

A. An indexed access method is always faster than accessing a table without the index.

This statement is incorrect. While indexes are designed to speed up data retrieval for specific queries, an indexed access method is not always faster than accessing a table without an index.

Full Table Scans: For queries that retrieve a large percentage of rows from a table, a full table scan can be faster than an index scan because it avoids the overhead of reading index blocks in addition to table blocks and often uses multiblock I/O efficiently.
Small Tables: For very small tables, a full table scan might be faster or equally fast, as the overhead of index lookup might outweigh the benefits.
DML Operations: Indexes can actually slow down DML operations (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) because the index must also be maintained whenever the table data changes.
B. An index always stores the keys in ascending order.

This statement is incorrect. While indexes often store keys in ascending order by default, you can specify the descending order for individual columns within an index when creating it. For example: CREATE INDEX emp_idx ON employees (last_name ASC, salary DESC);. This allows for efficient retrieval for queries requiring data sorted in mixed ascending/descending order.

C. Multiple indexes can be created on the same column.

This statement is incorrect. You cannot create multiple B-tree indexes on the exact same set of columns and in the same order. If you try to create a second index on (column_A, column_B) when one already exists, Oracle will prevent it because it‘s redundant. However, you can have:

Multiple indexes on different combinations of columns that might include the same column (e.g., (col_A, col_B) and (col_A, col_C)).
Different types of indexes on the same column (e.g., a B-tree index and a bitmap index).
Indexes on the same column with different sort orders (e.g., (col_A ASC) and (col_A DESC)). The statement “Multiple indexes can be created on the same column“ is broadly true if interpreted as a column being part of multiple indexes, but not multiple identical indexes. However, the intent of such a question in an exam usually refers to creating identical indexes, which is not allowed. Given the wording, the nuance implies you can‘t have two completely separate, distinct indexes just on EMP_ID if one already exists.

Correct:

D. A foreign key value in a child table column must match a key value in its parent table‘s primary or unique key column.

This statement is correct. This is the fundamental definition of a foreign key constraint. It enforces referential integrity, ensuring that a value in the foreign key column(s) of the child table either matches an existing value in the primary or unique key column(s) of the parent table, or is NULL (unless the foreign key column is also defined as NOT NULL).

questions.question_html:
Question 6 of 20
6. Question

Which statements are true about Deferred Segment Creation in Oracle Databases? (Choose two)

  • 1.
  • 2.
  • 3.
  • 4.
  • 5.
Correct

Correct:

A. If it is set to true at the instance level, then no sessions can have immediate segment creation.
This statement is correct. The DEFERRED_SEGMENT_CREATION initialization parameter (which can be set at the system/instance level) controls the default behavior. If it‘s set to TRUE at the instance level, then new tables (and their associated LOB segments) will generally defer segment creation until the first row is inserted. While you can override this for specific tables using SEGMENT CREATION IMMEDIATE in the CREATE TABLE statement, the default behavior for all sessions will be deferred. The phrasing “no sessions can have immediate segment creation“ is slightly ambiguous, but it refers to the default behavior for new objects created within those sessions, implying that explicit overrides are still possible for individual objects, not that the ability to create immediate segments is completely removed. However, if the question implies a universal default without exceptions, then yes, the default for new objects in all sessions would be deferred.

E. It is the default behavior for tables.
This statement is correct. Starting with Oracle Database 11g Release 2, DEFERRED_SEGMENT_CREATION is set to TRUE by default. This means that when you create a new table, Oracle creates the table object in the data dictionary but does not allocate any disk space (segment) for it until the first row of data is inserted. This saves space, especially for applications that create many tables that might remain empty for a long time.

Incorrect:

B. It is the default behavior for indexes.
This statement is incorrect. Deferred segment creation applies to tables and their associated LOB segments. It is not the default behavior for indexes. When an index is created, its segment is created immediately, regardless of the DEFERRED_SEGMENT_CREATION parameter.

C. It can be set only at the session level.
This statement is incorrect. The DEFERRED_SEGMENT_CREATION parameter can be set at the system/instance level (in the SPFILE or PFILE) using ALTER SYSTEM, and it can also be overridden at the session level using ALTER SESSION SET DEFERRED_SEGMENT_CREATION = {TRUE | FALSE};.

D. It is the default behavior for views.
This statement is incorrect. Views are logical objects that do not store any data themselves and thus do not have segments. Therefore, deferred segment creation is irrelevant for views. Segments are allocated only for physical storage objects like tables, indexes, and materialized views.

questions.preview: Which statements are true about joins? (Choose two)
questions.question_html:
Question 7 of 20
7. Question

Which statements are true about joins? (Choose two)

  • 1.
  • 2.
  • 3.
  • 4.
  • 5.
Correct

Correct:

D. Columns being joined must have the same name when using a NATURAL JOIN.

This statement is correct. A NATURAL JOIN automatically joins two tables based on all columns that have the same name and data type in both tables. You do not specify join conditions in the ON or USING clause; Oracle infers them from the common column names. If there are no common columns, a Cartesian product results.

E. A SELF JOIN can be a RIGHT OUTER JOIN.

This statement is correct. A SELF JOIN is simply a join where a table is joined to itself. This can be achieved using any join type (INNER, LEFT OUTER, RIGHT OUTER, FULL OUTER). By giving the table different aliases, you can treat it as two separate tables in the join. For example, you might use a RIGHT OUTER JOIN in a self-join to find employees who do not have a manager.

Incorrect:

A. A FULL OUTER JOIN excludes returning rows returned by an INNER JOIN.

This statement is incorrect. A FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from the left table and all rows from the right table, including rows that match the join condition (which are the rows an INNER JOIN would return) and rows that do not match. It‘s essentially the union of a LEFT OUTER JOIN and a RIGHT OUTER JOIN. It includes the inner join results.

questions.preview: Which statements are true about roles? (Choose two)
questions.question_html:
Question 8 of 20
8. Question

Which statements are true about roles? (Choose two)

  • 1.
  • 2.
  • 3.
  • 4.
  • 5.
Correct

Correct:

A. Roles can have passwords.
This statement is correct. Oracle allows you to secure roles with passwords using the IDENTIFIED BY password clause during role creation or alteration. When a role has a password, a user must explicitly SET ROLE role_name IDENTIFIED BY password; to enable that role, even if it has been granted to them.

C. Multiple roles can be granted to the same user.
This statement is correct. A single user can be granted multiple roles. This is a fundamental feature of Oracle‘s security model, allowing DBAs to organize privileges into logical groups (roles) and then grant those roles to users, simplifying privilege management.

Incorrect:

B. All roles granted to a user are always enabled by default when they log in.
This statement is incorrect. While roles granted to a user are generally enabled by default upon login, there are exceptions:

Roles with passwords: As mentioned in option A, roles with passwords are not enabled by default; they must be explicitly enabled by the user.
Default roles: A user can be assigned a subset of their granted roles as DEFAULT ROLES. Only these default roles (and any non-default roles that are not password-protected) are enabled automatically at login. Other non-default roles must be explicitly enabled using SET ROLE.
D. Roles can be granted object privileges only.
This statement is incorrect. Roles can be granted both system privileges (e.g., CREATE TABLE, SELECT ANY TABLE, UNLIMITED TABLESPACE) and object privileges (e.g., SELECT ON hr.employees, UPDATE ON sales.orders). Roles are a versatile mechanism for bundling any type of privilege.

E. Roles are unable to be granted to other roles.
This statement is incorrect. Roles can absolutely be granted to other roles. This allows for a hierarchical structure of privileges, where a higher-level role can inherit all privileges of lower-level roles, further simplifying complex privilege management. For example, a DBA_ROLE could be granted DEVELOPER_ROLE and OPERATOR_ROLE.

questions.preview: Which statements are true about sequences in a single instance Oracle Database?
questions.question_html:
Question 9 of 20
9. Question

Which statements are true about sequences in a single instance Oracle Database? (Choose two)

  • 1.
  • 2.
  • 3.
  • 4.
  • 5.
Correct

Correct:

A. A sequence can wrap around and start over again after reaching its maximum value.

This statement is correct. If a sequence is created with the CYCLE option, it will, after reaching its MAXVALUE (for an ascending sequence) or MINVALUE (for a descending sequence), wrap around and start generating values from its MINVALUE or MAXVALUE respectively.

E. A sequence‘s cached values can age out of the shared pool.

This statement is correct. When a sequence is created with the CACHE option, a specified number of sequence values are pre-allocated and stored in the Shared Pool (part of the SGA) to improve performance by reducing I/O and latch contention during value generation. If these cached values are not used for a period, they can be aged out of the Shared Pool due to memory pressure or LRU (Least Recently Used) algorithm, just like other objects in the Shared Pool. This means that if the instance shuts down or the cached values are aged out, the next time NEXTVAL is called, the sequence might “jump“ by more than its INCREMENT BY value because the remaining cached values are lost.

Incorrect:

B. A session attempting to select a sequence‘s NEXTVAL at the same time as another session, will wait on a row lock.

This statement is incorrect. Sequence number generation is an extremely fast and highly concurrent operation. Oracle uses a latch mechanism to serialize access to the sequence in the Shared Pool, not row locks. Sessions contending for a sequence will wait on a latch, not a row lock. Sequence generation is designed to avoid typical data locking issues for high concurrency.

C. When a sequence reaches its maximum value, it is always necessary to drop and re-create it.

This statement is incorrect. If a sequence reaches its maximum value, and it was not created with the CYCLE option, it will stop generating values. In this case, you can either:

Alter the sequence to increase its MAXVALUE.
Alter the sequence to enable the CYCLE option (if appropriate for the application).
Only if neither of these options is suitable, you might then drop and re-create it. It‘s not always necessary to drop and re-create.
D. Selecting a sequence‘s NEXTVAL always returns a number that is greater by one than the sequence‘s CURVAL.

This statement is incorrect.

NEXTVAL returns the next available sequence number.
CURRVAL returns the most recently generated sequence number for the current session. The crucial point is the INCREMENT BY value. NEXTVAL returns a number that is greater by the INCREMENT BY value (which defaults to 1) than the last number generated by the sequence globally, not necessarily CURRVAL. CURRVAL is session-specific. If INCREMENT BY is 5, NEXTVAL will return a number 5 greater than the previously generated number. Also, if cached values are lost (e.g., instance crash), the jump can be larger. The relationship is NEXTVAL = previous_value_generated + INCREMENT BY, and CURRVAL is just the NEXTVAL that was last obtained by this session.

This means that if the instance shuts down or the cached values are aged out, the next time NEXTVAL is called, the sequence might “jump“ by more than its INCREMENT BY value because the remaining cached values are lost.

Incorrect:

B. A session attempting to select a sequence‘s NEXTVAL at the same time as another session, will wait on a row lock.

This statement is incorrect. Sequence number generation is an extremely fast and highly concurrent operation. Oracle uses a latch mechanism to serialize access to the sequence in the Shared Pool, not row locks. Sessions contending for a sequence will wait on a latch, not a row lock. Sequence generation is designed to avoid typical data locking issues for high concurrency.

This statement is incorrect. If a sequence reaches its maximum value, and it was not created with the CYCLE option, it will stop generating values. In this case, you can either:

Alter the sequence to increase its MAXVALUE.
Alter the sequence to enable the CYCLE option (if appropriate for the application).
Only if neither of these options is suitable, you might then drop and re-create it. It‘s not always necessary to drop and re-create.

This statement is incorrect.

CURRVAL returns the most recently generated sequence number for the current session. The crucial point is the INCREMENT BY value. NEXTVAL returns a number that is greater by the INCREMENT BY value (which defaults to 1) than the last number generated by the sequence globally, not necessarily CURRVAL. CURRVAL is session-specific. The relationship is NEXTVAL = previous_value_generated + INCREMENT BY, and CURRVAL is just the NEXTVAL that was last obtained by this session.

questions.preview: Which are the benefits of external tables? (Choose two)
questions.question_html:
Question 10 of 20
10. Question

Which are the benefits of external tables? (Choose two)

  • 1.
  • 2.
  • 3.
  • 4.
  • 5.
Correct

Correct:

A. ORACLE LOADER type external tables allow data to be loaded and transformed in one operation when a CREATE TABLE…AS SELECT statement selects from an external table and creates a conventional heap table in an Oracle tablespace.

This statement is correct. An ORACLE_LOADER type external table acts as a read-only interface to data stored in external flat files. By using CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT (CTAS) on an external table, you effectively perform a direct path load of the data from the flat file into a new conventional Oracle table. This process can include transformations (e.g., in the SELECT clause) and filtering (e.g., with a WHERE clause), making it a powerful and efficient way to load and process external data.

E. DATA PUMP type external tables facilitate transporting the results of joins and complex aggregations of data from one database to another.

This statement is correct. DATA PUMP type external tables are primarily used as a staging mechanism for the Data Pump utility (expdp and impdp). You can use them to:

Unload data from Oracle to a flat file: CREATE TABLE … ORGANIZATION EXTERNAL (TYPE ORACLE_DATAPUMP … ) AS SELECT … allows you to export the results of any complex query (including joins, aggregations, subqueries) into a Data Pump format file.
Load data into Oracle from a Data Pump file: They provide an interface for Data Pump to read from. This makes them highly beneficial for transporting complex datasets between Oracle databases, especially for data transformation and migration scenarios where you don‘t want to export full tables.
Incorrect:

B. DATA PUMP type external tables allow the DATA PUMP utility to import data into flat files in a file system that is accessible to the Oracle owner.

This statement is partially misleading and incorrect. While DATA PUMP type external tables do interact with flat files, their primary purpose is for exporting from the database into Data Pump format files (e.g., using CREATE TABLE … ORGANIZATION EXTERNAL AS SELECT …). The DATA PUMP utility then imports data from these Data Pump format files into the database. It‘s not typically used to “import data into flat files,“ but rather to manage the flow of data via these intermediate Data Pump files. The statement mixes up the direction and primary use.

C. Both ORACLE LOADER and DATA PUMP type external tables can be created with the CREATE TABLE…AS SELECT statement.

This statement is incorrect. While ORACLE_DATAPUMP type external tables are indeed created with CREATE TABLE … AS SELECT (when exporting data), ORACLE_LOADER type external tables are not typically created with CREATE TABLE…AS SELECT. Instead, ORACLE_LOADER external tables are created with CREATE TABLE … ORGANIZATION EXTERNAL (TYPE ORACLE_LOADER …) LOCATION (‘filename‘) and point to existing flat files. Their purpose is to read from external files, not to generate them from a SELECT statement directly.

D. ORACLE LOADER type external tables do not support CTAS because they are mainly designed for reading and transforming data from external sources, not for creating new tables from query results.

This statement is incorrect. As explained in option A, ORACLE_LOADER type external tables do support CTAS (CREATE TABLE…AS SELECT). This is a common and powerful technique to load data from an external file into a conventional Oracle table while optionally applying transformations and filtering, effectively creating a new table from the query results of the external table.

questions.preview: Which statements are true about row chaining and row migration in Oracle Databas
questions.question_html:
Question 11 of 20
11. Question

Which statements are true about row chaining and row migration in Oracle Databases? (Choose two)

  • 1.
  • 2.
  • 3.
  • 4.
  • 5.
Correct

Correct:

A migrated row can also be chained.
Chained rows are always used for each row when there are more than 255 columns in a heap table.

Explanation for “A migrated row can also be chained.“ (This is implicitly correct based on the understanding of both concepts)

Row Migration: Occurs when an UPDATE operation increases the size of a row such that it no longer fits in its original block. Oracle moves the entire row to a new block, leaving a pointer (forwarding address) in the old block.
Row Chaining: Occurs when a row is too large to fit into a single data block, either at the time of INSERT or subsequent UPDATE. The row is then stored in multiple row pieces, which are “chained“ together across different blocks.
Why it‘s true: A row might initially fit in a block but then be updated and migrate to a new block. If, at the same time, the updated row becomes so large that it still cannot fit entirely within that new block, it can then become chained across multiple blocks, even in its migrated state. Thus, a migrated row can indeed be chained.

Explanation for “Chained rows are always used for each row when there are more than 255 columns in a heap table.“ (Explicitly supported by the provided Oracle documentation excerpts)

Oracle 10g Concepts: “When a table has more than 255 columns, rows that have data after the 255th column are likely to be chained within the same block. This is called intra-block chaining… If the row fits in the block, users do not see an effect in I/O performance…“
Oracle 19c Concepts: “Oracle Database can only store 255 columns in a row piece. Thus, if you insert a row into a table that has 1000 columns, then the database creates 4 row pieces, typically chained over multiple blocks.“

Both documentation snippets confirm that a fundamental limitation of Oracle‘s row piece structure is 255 columns. If a table has more than 255 columns, a single row will inherently need to be split into multiple “row pieces,“ which are then chained together. questions.question_html:
Question 12 of 20
12. Question

Which statements are true about Resumable Space Allocation and its processing in Oracle Databases? (Choose two)

  • 1.
  • 2.
  • 3.
  • 4.
  • 5.
Correct

Correct:

B. It can be triggered when a datafile is waiting for an autoextend operation to complete.

This statement is correct. Resumable Space Allocation pauses a session‘s DML or DDL operation if it encounters a space allocation error. One such error can occur when a datafile needs to autoextend but is waiting for the underlying operating system to complete the allocation, or if there‘s an issue preventing the autoextend. In such a scenario, the session can be suspended, allowing the DBA to address the underlying space issue.

C. It can be triggered due to exceeding a tablespace‘s space quota.

This statement is correct. A common scenario for Resumable Space Allocation to be triggered is when a user attempts to create or extend an object (e.g., insert rows into a table) but exceeds their assigned space quota on a tablespace. Instead of immediately failing, the session can be suspended, giving the DBA an opportunity to increase the user‘s quota or free up space.

Incorrect:

A. It works only for Locally Managed tablespaces.

This statement is incorrect. Resumable Space Allocation is a database feature that works for both Locally Managed Tablespaces (LMTs) and the older Dictionary Managed Tablespaces (DMTs), although DMTs are generally deprecated. The feature‘s ability to suspend operations upon space errors is not limited to a specific tablespace management type.

D. It can be triggered due to reaching a segment‘s maximum extents limit.

This statement is incorrect. Resumable Space Allocation is designed to handle space allocation errors like “out of space in tablespace,“ “quota exceeded,“ or “maximum extents reached on a tablespace“ (if an individual segment grows to exhaust the tablespace). However, it does not specifically handle reaching a segment‘s maximum extents limit as a trigger for suspension itself. The maximum extents limit for a segment is usually a hard limit set during table/index creation (though in modern Oracle, UNLIMITED extents are common for LMTs). When this limit is hit, it typically results in an ORA-01631 error, and the operation fails, rather than being suspended by Resumable Space Allocation. Resumable operations are more about the tablespace running out of space or the user running out of quota.

E. It works only for Dictionary Managed tablespaces.

This statement is incorrect. Similar to option A, Resumable Space Allocation works for both Locally Managed and Dictionary Managed tablespaces, not exclusively for DMTs. LMTs are the recommended and default tablespace type in modern Oracle versions.

questions.preview: Which are true about all dynamic performance views? (Choose two)
questions.question_html:
Question 13 of 20
13. Question

Which are true about all dynamic performance views? (Choose two)

  • 1.
  • 2.
  • 3.
  • 4.
  • 5.
  • 6.
Correct

Correct:

B. They can display metadata from the buffer caches.
This is correct. Dynamic performance views provide real-time information about the instance‘s activity. For example, V$SEGMENT_STATISTICS can show buffer gets for segments, and V$LATCH can show latch contention related to buffer cache access. Views like V$BH (Buffer Headers) provide detailed information about blocks in the buffer cache.

F. They can display metadata from the SGA.
This is a fundamental characteristic of dynamic performance views (V$). Their data is directly populated from the System Global Area (SGA) and other volatile memory structures (like the PGA for session-specific data) that reflect the current state and activity of the running Oracle instance. Examples include V$SGA (SGA size and components), V$SESSION (session information residing in SGA), V$SYSSTAT (system statistics stored in SGA), and V$SQL (SQL statement statistics in the Shared Pool, which is part of SGA).

Incorrect:

A. They always display rows for every query even when the database is in NOMOUNT state.
This statement is incorrect. While some very basic V$ views related to the instance itself might be accessible in NOMOUNT state (e.g., V$PARAMETER, V$INSTANCE), many critical V$ views that require the database to be mounted or open (like V$DATABASE, V$DATAFILE, V$SQL, V$SESSION) will not display meaningful rows or might not be accessible at all in NOMOUNT state because the database structure (control files, datafiles) is not yet known.

C. They can display metadata from the data dictionary.
This statement is incorrect. Dynamic performance views (V$) provide information about the current state and activity of the instance. questions.preview: Where can metadata about Oracle Database users and privileges be stored for use
questions.question_html:
Question 14 of 20
14. Question

Where can metadata about Oracle Database users and privileges be stored for use by authentication processing? (Choose two)

  • 1.
  • 2.
  • 3.
  • 4.
  • 5.
Correct

Correct:

B. In the password file

The password file (orapw) stores password credentials for administrative users (like SYS, SYSTEM, SYSDG, SYSBACKUP, SYSRAC, SYSKM) who connect with SYSDBA, SYSOPER, etc., privileges, especially for connections where the database itself is not yet open (e.g., STARTUP). It allows for remote administration and authentication without the database being fully up. It‘s a specific, separate file used before the database dictionary is fully available.

E. In the SYSTEM tablespace

This is the primary location for metadata about Oracle Database users, roles, and privileges for regular database operations. The SYSTEM tablespace contains the data dictionary, which is a collection of base tables and views that store all metadata about the database. This includes:

User definitions (USER$, TS$, ENC$)
Role definitions
System and object privileges granted to users and roles (OBJAUTH$, SYS_AUTH$) When a regular user connects and authenticates, Oracle queries these data dictionary tables in the SYSTEM tablespace.
Incorrect:

A. In the SYSAUX tablespace

The SYSAUX tablespace is a mandatory auxiliary tablespace that stores data for various database components and features that previously required their own tablespaces (e.g., AWR, Optimizer Statistics, SQL Management Base, Enterprise Manager repository). While it contains a lot of database metadata and operational data, it does not directly store user authentication or privilege metadata that is explicitly used by the core authentication process. That core metadata resides in the SYSTEM tablespace.

C. “In the control file“

The control file stores critical metadata about the physical structure of the database (e.g., names and locations of datafiles, redo log files, archived logs, database name, checkpoint information, RMAN backup records). It does not store user definitions or privilege information for authentication.

D. In the SPFILE

The SPFILE (Server Parameter File) stores the initialization parameters for the database instance. It defines how the instance starts up and operates (e.g., memory allocation, file paths, character set). It does not store user accounts or privilege grants. Those are managed within the database‘s data dictionary (primarily in the SYSTEM tablespace).

questions.preview: Which statements automatically commit when they complete successfully? (Choose t
questions.question_html:
Question 15 of 20
15. Question

Which statements automatically commit when they complete successfully? (Choose two)

  • 1.
  • 2.
  • 3.
  • 4.
  • 5.
Correct

Correct:

C. CREATE TABLE AS SELECT statements with no WHERE clause
D. CREATE TABLE…AS SELECT statements with a WHERE clause

DDL (Data Definition Language) statements (e.g., CREATE TABLE AS SELECT) automatically commit upon successful execution.

This includes both forms of the statement:

CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (with or without a WHERE clause).

CREATE TABLE…AS SELECT (with or without a WHERE clause).

DDL statements perform an implicit commit before and after execution.

Incorrect:

A. DELETE FROM TABLE statements with a WHERE clause

DELETE is a DML (Data Manipulation Language) statement.

DML operations require an explicit COMMIT (or rollback) to finalize changes.

No automatic commit occurs.

B. INSERT INTO…SELECT FROM statements

Like DELETE, INSERT INTO…SELECT is a DML statement.

Changes are not committed automaticallymust issue COMMIT manually.

E. DELETE FROM TABLE statements with no WHERE clause

Even a DELETE without a WHERE clause (which deletes all rows) is still DML.

No auto-committransaction remains active until COMMIT/ROLLBACK.

Question 16 of 20
16. Question

Which is one of the situations causing a transaction that has already updated several rows to commit?

  • 1.
  • 2.
  • 3.
  • 4.
  • 5.
Correct

Correct:

D. When a DDL statement is executed successfully in the same session.

This statement is correct. In Oracle, a successful execution of a DDL (Data Definition Language) statement (such as CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP INDEX, TRUNCATE TABLE, CREATE USER, GRANT etc.) implicitly performs a COMMIT operation on any pending DML (Data Manipulation Language) changes in the current session. This is because DDL operations modify the data dictionary, and Oracle ensures that the data dictionary changes are part of a committed transaction.

Incorrect:

A. When a SAVEPOINT is created by the session.

A SAVEPOINT is a marker within a transaction that allows for partial rollbacks. It does not commit the transaction. You can roll back to a savepoint without ending the entire transaction.

B. When a DML statement is executed successfully in the same session.

A successful execution of a DML (Data Manipulation Language) statement (such as INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE) does not implicitly commit a transaction. DML statements are part of a transaction that must be explicitly committed (COMMIT) or rolled back (ROLLBACK).

C. When a DDL statement is executed successfully by the same user in a different session.

A DDL statement executed in a different session will implicitly commit any pending DML changes in that specific different session, but it will not commit DML changes in the original session. Transactions are session-specific.

E. When a DML statement is executed successfully by the same user in a different session.

Similar to option C, a DML statement executed in a different session does not affect or commit a transaction in the original session. Transactions are isolated to the session in which they are initiated.

questions.question_html:
Question 17 of 20
17. Question

Which statements are true about Oracle initialization parameter files? (Choose four)

  • 1.
  • 2.
  • 3.
  • 4.
  • 5.
  • 6.
Correct

Correct:

A. SPFILES can be created from memory.
This statement is correct. An SPFILE can be created from the current in-memory parameter settings of a running instance using the command CREATE SPFILE FROM MEMORY;. This is useful if you‘ve made dynamic changes to parameters in memory and want to persist them to an SPFILE.

C. PFILES can be created from memory when the database is in MOUNT state.
This statement is correct. A PFILE can be created from the current in-memory parameter settings using the command CREATE PFILE FROM MEMORY;. This command can be executed even if the database is in MOUNT state, as the instance is up and its memory parameters are accessible.

D. PFILES can be created from SPFILES when the database is in MOUNT state.
This statement is correct. You can create a PFILE from an existing SPFILE using the command CREATE PFILE FROM SPFILE;. This operation requires the instance to be started (so it can read the SPFILE), and it can be performed in MOUNT state.

F. SPFILES can be created from PFILES when the database is open.
This statement is correct. An SPFILE can be created from a PFILE using the command CREATE SPFILE FROM PFILE;. This command can be executed while the database is OPEN, MOUNTED, or even in NOMOUNT state (if you‘re creating a new SPFILE for a future startup).

Incorrect:

B. PFILES are part text and part binary files.
This statement is incorrect. PFILES (Parameter Files) are plain text files that can be viewed and edited with a standard text editor. They are not binary files or a mix of text and binary.

E. SPFILES cannot be created from PFILES when the database is in NOMOUNT state.
This statement is incorrect. An SPFILE can be created from a PFILE when the database is in NOMOUNT state. The instance is up, and it can read the PFILE to create the binary SPFILE. For example, STARTUP NOMOUNT PFILE=‘path/to/my_pfile.ora‘; CREATE SPFILE FROM PFILE;. This is a common practice when first converting from a PFILE to an SPFILE setup.

questions.question_html:
Question 18 of 20
18. Question

You execute this command:

SQL
CREATE SMALLFILE TABLESPACE SMALL_TBSP
DATAFILE ‘/u01/oracle/data/small_f1.dbf‘
SIZE 20G;

Sufficient storage is available in the file system /U01. There are bufffer caches for 8K,16K, and 32K blocksizes. Which statements are true about the SMALL_TBSP tablespace? (Choose two)

  • 1.
  • 2.
  • 3.
  • 4.
  • 5.
Correct

Correct :
1. It is a locally managed tablespace.
2. The blocksize is determined by the DB_BLOCK_SIZE parameter setting used when the database was created.

 For “It is a locally managed tablespace.“
1. “All tablespaces in Oracle 10g and later (except SYSTEM) are locally managed by default.“
2. “Oracle does not create dictionary-managed tablespaces anymore, unless explicitly specified (which is not done here).“
3. “The CREATE TABLESPACE command without SEGMENT SPACE MANAGEMENT specification defaults to locally managed tablespaces.“
This explanation clearly states that in modern Oracle versions, tablespaces are locally managed by default unless explicitly configured otherwise. The provided CREATE TABLESPACE command doesn‘t include any specific settings to make it dictionary-managed, so it will be locally managed.
 For “The blocksize is determined by the DB_BLOCK_SIZE parameter setting used when the database was created.“
1. “When no block size is specified in CREATE TABLESPACE, Oracle defaults to the database‘s default block size, which is set by the DB_BLOCK_SIZE parameter.“
2. “To check the database block size: SHOW PARAMETER DB_BLOCK_SIZE;“
3. “If the database was created with an 8K block size, then this tablespace will also have an 8K block size.“
4. “If a different block size is desired, it must be explicitly stated in the CREATE TABLESPACE command: CREATE TABLESPACE SMALL_TBSP DATAFILE ‘/u01/oracle/data/small_f1.dbf‘ SIZE 20G BLOCKSIZE 16K; “
5. “Since the command did not specify BLOCKSIZE, it defaults to DB_BLOCK_SIZE.“
This explanation confirms that if the CREATE TABLESPACE statement doesn‘t include a BLOCKSIZE clause, the tablespace inherits the database‘s default block size, which is determined by the DB_BLOCK_SIZE initialization parameter.
 Why the other options are incorrect:
? “It can never exceed 20 gigabytes.“
§ Explanation provided: “1. The initial size is 20GB, but Oracle allows adding more datafiles to a smallfile tablespace. 2. Smallfile tablespaces can contain multiple datafiles, each up to 32TB (depending on the block size). 3. Example: ALTER DATABASE SMALL_TBSP ADD DATAFILE ‘/u01/oracle/data/small_f2.dbf‘ SIZE 10G; 4. Thus, it is incorrect to say the tablespace can never exceed 20GB.“ This clearly shows that you can add more datafiles to a smallfile tablespace, so it‘s not limited to the initial size.
? “It must be smaller than the biggest bigfile tablespaces in the same database.“ and “It must be smaller than all bigfile tablespaces in the same database.“
§ Explanation provided: “1. The size of a smallfile tablespace is independent of bigfile tablespaces. 2. There is no restriction stating that a smallfile tablespace must be smaller than the largest bigfile tablespace in the database.“ and “1. Similar to Option C, a smallfile tablespace can be larger than some bigfile tablespaces. 2. The size of a smallfile tablespace is not dependent on the size of bigfile tablespaces in the database.“ These options are incorrect because the sizes of smallfile and bigfile tablespaces are independent.
? “It definitely has a 16K blocksize.“
§ Explanation provided: “1. The block size of a tablespace is determined by the DB_BLOCK_SIZE parameter, unless explicitly specified using the BLOCKSIZE clause. 2. Since no block size is specified in the CREATE TABLESPACE statement, it defaults to DB_BLOCK_SIZE (typically 8K). 3. It could have a 16K block size only if explicitly set, but this is not confirmed in the provided statement.“ This option is incorrect because the block size defaults to the database‘s DB_BLOCK_SIZE, which is not necessarily 16K.

2. The blocksize is determined by the DB_BLOCK_SIZE parameter setting used when the database was created.

questions.question_html:
Question 19 of 20
19. Question

Which statement is true about the COUNT function?

  • 1.
  • 2.
  • 3.
  • 4.
  • 5.
Correct

Correct :
COUNT(*) can be used together with other columns in a select list and a GROUP BY clause to return the total number of rows for each group.

 For the Correct Option:
1. “The COUNT(*) function counts all rows, including those with NULL values.“ This is a fundamental property of COUNT(*).
2. “When used with GROUP BY, it returns the count for each group.“ This explains its behavior when combined with GROUP BY.
3. “Example: SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY department_id;“ This provides a clear, runnable example demonstrating how COUNT(*) with GROUP BY correctly returns the total number of rows (employees) for each group (department).

For the Incorrect Options, the provided text explains why they are false:
? “COUNT(DISTINCT COLX) returns the number of distinct values in COLX including NULLS.“
§ Explanation provided: “1. COUNT(DISTINCT COLX) excludes NULL values.“ This directly contradicts the statement in the option, making the option false.
? “A SELECT statement with COUNT(DISTINCT COLX) must include the GROUP BY clause.“
§ Explanation provided: “1. COUNT(DISTINCT COLX) does not require GROUP BY. 2. It simply counts unique non-null values in COLX.“ This clarifies that GROUP BY is optional for COUNT(DISTINCT COLX) if you want a single distinct count for the whole table.
? “COUNT(*) can be used only to return the total number of rows in a table.“
§ Explanation provided: “1. COUNT() can count rows in entire tables or within groups. 2. Example with filtering: SELECT COUNT() FROM employees WHERE salary > 5000;“ This shows that COUNT(*) can be used with WHERE clauses to count subsets of rows, not just the entire table.
? “A SELECT statement with COUNT(DISTINCT COLX) must include the HAVING clause.“
Explanation provided: “1. HAVING is only needed to filter results after aggregation.“ This correctly states the purpose of HAVING and clarifies that it‘s not a mandatory clause for COUNT(DISTINCT COLX) itself.

questions.preview: You start your database instance by using the STARTUP MOUNT command after an ins
questions.question_html:
Question 20 of 20
20. Question

You start your database instance by using the STARTUP MOUNT command after an instance failure. Which are true about the processing that is performed? (Choose two)

  • 1.
  • 2.
  • 3.
  • 4.
  • 5.
  • 6.
Correct

Correct:

D. When an instance is started, memory for the SGA, including the buffer cache, is allocated.

This is correct. Regardless of the startup mode (NOMOUNT, MOUNT, or OPEN), starting the Oracle instance involves allocating the System Global Area (SGA) in memory. The SGA includes the buffer cache, shared pool, redo log buffer, and other memory structures essential for the database instance to operate.

E. The STARTUP MOUNT command opens the control files.

This is also correct. The STARTUP MOUNT command starts the instance and then mounts the database. Mounting the database involves opening the control files. The control files contain metadata about the database‘s physical structure (datafile names and locations, redo log file names, etc.). The instance needs this information to proceed.

Incorrect:

A. Tempfiles are created when the database is opened.

Tempfiles (used by temporary tablespaces) are usually created when the tablespace is created, not when the database is opened. The STARTUP MOUNT command does not involve creating or managing tempfiles.

B. The listener is a separate process and is not started by the STARTUP MOUNT command.

This is correct. The Listener is a separate Oracle Net Services process that listens for incoming client connection requests. It is started and managed independently of the database instance startup process. STARTUP MOUNT does not start the Listener.

C. Datafile consistency is checked when the database is opened, not mounted.

Datafile consistency is checked during the OPEN phase, but a limited check can also occur during the MOUNT phase. The MOUNT phase reads the control files, which contain information about the datafiles. While a full consistency check (like media recovery) is done when the database is opened, the MOUNT phase does verify that the datafiles listed in the control file are present and accessible. So, the statement is partially incorrect.

F. The instance is started, and the control file has been opened, so the system user can log in.

While the instance is started and the control file is opened in MOUNT mode, the database is not open for general access. User connections are not allowed in MOUNT mode. The database must be explicitly opened (ALTER DATABASE OPEN;) before regular users can connect. Only after the OPEN command can users connect.

Incorrect

Correct:

D. When an instance is started, memory for the SGA, including the buffer cache, is allocated.

This is correct. Regardless of the startup mode (NOMOUNT, MOUNT, or OPEN), starting the Oracle instance involves allocating the System Global Area (SGA) in memory.
